03 Accumulation & Wealth Building

The 44 vs 64 Problem

A target-date fund treats your risk as a function of one number — your birth year. Your real risk depends on at least three.

The Planning LetterGlide Paths & Allocation

There is a quiet assumption baked into the most popular retirement product in America. A target-date fund — the default in millions of 401(k) plans — decides how much stock you should own based entirely on the year you intend to retire. Everyone aiming at 2045 gets the same glide path, the same descent from aggressive to cautious, regardless of how much they've saved, what else they own, or whether a 20% drop would make them sell at the worst possible moment.

For a default, that's reasonable engineering. A single dial that's roughly right for the average saver beats the paralysis of choosing nothing. But "roughly right for the average" is a low bar for the most important financial decision you'll make — the split between assets that grow and assets that protect. This letter is about reading your own glide path: what the automated version gets right, where it's blunt, and how to tell whether your portfolio is dressed for your actual life.

The Curve

What a glide path actually is

A glide path is simply the planned decline in your stock allocation as retirement approaches — the slow shift from growth (equities, which build wealth but lurch) to preservation (bonds and cash, which steady the ship but barely outrun inflation). The logic is sound: a 30-year-old has decades to recover from a crash, so volatility is just noise. A 65-year-old about to draw an income has no such luxury — a bad year now is a permanent dent.

The classic rule of thumb compresses this into one line: hold roughly (120 − your age)% in stocks. A target-date fund does something similar but smoother, and crucially, it holds a high equity stake far longer than older "100 − age" rules did, because we now expect to live — and spend — for three decades after we stop working.

The same portfolio cannot be correct for both — yet a single glide path quietly assumes a version of you that may not exist.

The Blunt Instrument

Where the target-date fund goes blunt

The flaw isn't the glide path's shape — it's that the shape responds to only one input: time until retirement. Two people retiring in 2045 receive identical allocations even when their realities couldn't be more different. One has a paid-off house, a pension, and three years of cash on hand. The other has none of these and a job that vanishes in every recession. The fund treats them as twins.

Sound allocation depends on two distinct things the birth-year dial can't see. The first is your risk capacity — your objective ability to absorb losses, set by your time horizon, the stability of your income, and the cushion of your other assets. The second is your risk tolerance — your emotional willingness to watch the number fall without flinching. They are not the same, and the gaps between them are where real damage happens.

Why It Matters

The same crash, two very different mornings

Abstractions about "20 points of equity" feel academic until a real bear market arrives. So put the 44-year-old's 76/24 portfolio and the 64-year-old's 56/44 portfolio through the worst year in living memory — 2008, when the S&P 500 fell about 37% and high-quality bonds rose about 5%.

None of this means abandoning the target-date fund. For many savers it remains an excellent, low-cost, hands-off default — far better than an unmanaged pile of guesses. The point is to use it knowingly: to check whether its one-size assumption fits your three-size reality, and to nudge it if it doesn't (for instance, by holding a fund dated a few years earlier or later than your literal retirement to shift the glide path more conservative or more aggressive).

Today's Move

Run a 10-minute allocation audit

Find out what you actually own versus what your age and temperament call for.

  1. Add up every investment account and calculate your real stock-vs-everything-else split. Most people are more concentrated in equities than they think.
  2. Compute your rule-of-thumb target: 120 minus your age in stocks. That's your starting reference, not gospel.
  3. Adjust for capacity: stable income, pension, paid-off home, or years of cash let you hold more stock than the rule; the opposite pushes you lower.
  4. Adjust for tolerance: if a 25% paper loss would genuinely make you sell, set your target to the more conservative of the two — own a portfolio you'll actually keep.
  5. If your actual split is more than ~10 points off your adjusted target, you've found your over-exposure. Rebalance gradually, mindful of taxes in taxable accounts.

The birth-year dial is a fine place to start and a poor place to stop. Your portfolio should reflect not just when you plan to retire, but how steady your income is, what else you own, and — the part no algorithm can measure — how you'll actually behave on the worst morning of the decade.

That closes our first section on building wealth. Next week we cross into the harder half of the journey — turning a pile of savings into a paycheck that lasts — beginning with the single most dangerous stretch of any retirement: the sequence-of-returns risk.
